utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Milosevic, you have for the witness this first hearing for you to examine on realistic matters, of course. Yes, it's for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zwaan, in your report you say that you are a sociologist and anthropologist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have no legal qualifications as a lawyer or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We also have the names of the employees and staff of the Centre for Holocaust and Genocide Studies and that it is a four-member team in Amsterdam; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And none of those individuals are legal men. Three are historians, and you yourself are a sociologist and anthropologist. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, isn't it a little unusual that a centre for research into Holocaust and genocide or genocide studies don't have any lawyers, because genocide is a legal category, is it not, in the first place?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can consider genocide as a legal category. That's one, but you can also see it as a historical phenomenon or as a sociological phenomenon. It's quite usual, by the way, that centres of genocide and Holocaust studies over the world do not have legal specialists because the juridical aspects practice are not first and foremost in the historical and sociological study of the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I am bearing in mind a fact which Mr. Nice did mention, actually, that for this composition the legal meaning is the only essential one, and that's why I'm asking you that. Now, in the last paragraph on page 6 of your report it says that the centre was officially opened in September 2003 with a public manifestation in the order of the university of Amsterdam. So your centre was in fact opened just four months ago; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The official opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your report was written on instruction from the other side, that is to say two months after the centre was established. Is that right, Mr. Zwaan?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have been working on it for several months, but it was finished after the centre was opened, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you personally within the frameworks of the centre have any other project that you've worked on except for this particular report?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what centre -- what were the other projects that the centre had, except this report of yours?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been teaching a master course for advanced students on the comparative study of genocide. That's one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you what other projects the centre has. Now your regular activity in the way of teaching is something else.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may consider that something else, but we at the centre see projects as well as in research as in teaching as in public discussions. I could name another project. We are organising a conference on the genocide in Rwanda which will take place in April. So we're starting on that and organising the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, as in your report you underline specifically when the centre was opened. There was a public manifestation in the Aula of the University of Amsterdam. I assume that you stress this as being an important fact, otherwise you wouldn't have stated it in your report. So what is the importance of that particular event, that manifestation that you have highlighted in that way in your report, except to impress, of course, the opening of the centre?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did not name it to impress anyone but just to introduce the centre and tell the reader when it was started and when it was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, how many written works do you have on the topic of genocide studies?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got about 10 to 12 articles and a rather hefty book of about 450 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This report was compiled at the request of Mr. Nice; is that right? That's what it says in paragraph 1 of the introduction.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it has been written at the request of the OTP. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning in sentence 1 of the introduction it says, and I quote: "The primary report of this report is to provide tools of analysis by reference to which the reader may understand how genocides and other mass crimes targeting specific groups can occur in human societies." Now, who is the reader you are targeting who is there to enter into analysis of how genocides come about?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is very simple. The answer is everybody who reads the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, speaking of the purpose, in paragraph 2 you say in the introduction, and I quote you: "I have been -- the OTP has been -- I understand from the OTP that this will enable the Chamber," and I assume you mean this Trial Chamber sitting across the way from you, "to consider the learning that exists in relation to genocide and to make such decisions about applying it to the facts of this case." Is that the purpose?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the purpose, yes, and it still is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- have heard of the principle known from Roman law, iuria novit curia.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. Maybe you can explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it means, in translation, that it is assumed that the court is well-versed in the law, and that is one of the central principles and necessary assumption for the functioning of every normal legal system, that the court is well acquainted with matters of law.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you not feel then that Mr. Nice in bringing you in as an expert witness has in mind teaching the Judges what genocide actually is? Do you not feel that that in a way - how shall I put this? - is contradictory to that principle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not -- just a moment, please. That's not a matter for the witness to answer that. That is a matter for us to decide, which we will do in due course. We've permitted this witness to give evidence. He can. What the witness can of course deal with is his part, but as far as matters of law are concerned, they are matters for the Judges, and you can address us in due course. But the witness is certainly entitled to answer that generally as far as he understands his role, his own personal role is concerned if he'd like to answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, very shortly. I think the question should be put to Mr. Nice, firstly. But secondly, I'd like to add that the report I've written is a historical and sociological report which tries to summarise the general insights which have been regarded in these disciplines in the processes of genocide. So I do not pretend, or wish, to go into any legal matters here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you do not wish to enter into any legal matters here. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Quite rightly. He's not here as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He is not a lawyer, and in due course you can address us on it when the accused can do so, but the witness is simply giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zwaan, the so-called Prosecution, as it says in the introduction, requested of you to exclude any mention of Bosnia or reference to Bosnia. Now, when you compiled the report did you nonetheless have in mind the positions and concept in relation to the alleged genocide in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether I understand your question correctly, but let me try. I wrote the report based on the four cases I mention in the report, and I've tried to summarise insights into genocidal processes in general. I do not think that the Bosnian case, as we could call it that, was at the foremost of my mind when I wrote the report, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zwaan. Now, in your analysis, you considered in general terms this subject, and the annihilation of the Jews, the Armenians; that was the second case you looked at. And Cambodia, and Rwanda. Those four cases. Those were the ones that you considered; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you emphasised in the introduction to your report that they requested that you exclude all reference to Bosnia. Now, tell me, as you deal with the phenomenon as such and you have taken as your basis these particular cases or instances, you are a Dutchman yourself. Did it ever occur to you to include the case of Holland, for example? If they said exclude Bosnia, what about Holland? Did they say exclude all reference to Holland?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not say so. But just to inform you, I've written a very extensive article about the uses of political violence in Dutch history.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Well, if you've written that article, then you know that as at the beginning of the 17th century when Holland set up the West India and East India company, the two Dutch companies, that it was under the auspices of the Dutch government that the two companies had the right to use armed forces -- I'll call it to use the armed forces of Holland; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, although I'm not quite sure whether we should descent into the colonial history of the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the question is the phenomenon of genocide. That is the subject you are analysing, and you know that Holland systematically exterminated regions from their local inhabitants. Take the case of Africa, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is -- this is -- we're going well away from our relevant matter. The witness has given his evidence in the very limited, to some extent, in the area, so rather than going into that old history, there's no point going over it again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, if you bring this down to the 20th century alone and limit it to that, then I can restrict myself to the 20th century as well. However, as a consequence of the facts I mentioned previously, in the 20th century, for example, as you know full well, Holland was the founder of apartheid in 1948 when the Afrikaans party won in southern Africa. They induced this, and it lasted until about 10 years ago, and you know that very well, let alone the several hundred years --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. You've heard the area which the witness has dealt with and it's about that that you can deal with, rather than the broad history going back to the 16th century. We have not the time to do that, and it's not right to consider it. You can ask him about the matters which he's dealt with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going back to the 16th century, Mr. May, if I say that in the 20th century, saw that apartheid was founded and they are the founders of apartheid, let alone the fact that a vast number of slaves who were sent to the Caribbean countries were also the result of the genocide that was committed. So I asked, as we're talking about a Dutch centre, whether they dealt with subjects of that kind, because in Serbia, we have a saying that says "Sweep the dirt in front of your own house first."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we can ask the witness that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, maybe just very shortly. I think Dutch historians have done an enormous lot of research as well about the Dutch involvement with slavery in 16th and 17th century, and later they've also done a lot of research into apartheid. It was not founded by the Dutch government but by people who came from Dutch background far earlier in history, and there has been no responsibility whatsoever by the Dutch government for apartheid in South Africa. But I think the darker aspects of Dutch history have been studied thoroughly by Dutch historians and also by other historians. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if you have taken phenomena in the 20th century and looked at them, tell me, please, why have you omitted the genocide over the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether I understand your question. I was asked to write my report in a general sense and omit any reference to happenings on the Balkans, and so I did. So I did not dig into the tragic history of groups of Serbs during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zwaan. But do you know, since you spoke in your report about Nazism that this puppet state was created in the Second World War under the auspices of Hitler and Mussolini and it was called the Independent State of Croatia, and to all practical intents and purposes, it committed the greatest genocide in view of its size. And do you know that according to the facts and figures that the former Yugoslavia had and the president at the time, Josip Broz Tito, and he was a Croat, that 700.000 Serbs, including 30.000 Jews and Romanies, were exterminated in the Jasenovac camp and others for the mere fact that they had a different religion and were of a different ethnicity? And that is part of the questions that you study and deal with within the realm of those topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must ask this witness a question. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: Do you know that on the website of the Weisenthal Centre, for example, today you can find something that says that Jasenovac was the "[In English] Largest camp in Croatia between 1941 and 1945. Under department 3, Croatian security police, 600.000 people were murdered here, Serbs, Jews 30.000, Gypsy, and under the Ustasha regime." [No interpertation] Do you know about that fact?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly know about that fact. I do not agree with the figures named in the sources I have seen about this. I think the most reasonable estimate of the total amount of victims, including Jews, Serbs, and others, lies about between 100.000 and 120.000 people. So I would not agree with the amount of 600.000 people. On the other hand, I would like to add that this is something we discussed also yesterday, that the collective memory of these types of tragic events has played an important role also in present times. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you do not agree with the figures quoted on the official website centre of the Weisenthal Centre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has just answered the question, given his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the following definition of the Weisenthal Centre, and you can also find this on his website, he defines Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the concept of Ustashas, and I quote: "Created in 1930, Ustashas was a Croatian nationalist terrorist organisation. [In English] Its members' hatred of Jews was only rivaled by their hatred of the Serbs. Brought to power after Hitler created a Croatian puppet state in 1941, Ustasha terrorists killed 500.000 Serbs, expelled 250.000 and forced 250.000 to convert to Catholicism."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness must have the opportunity of responding to this. Is there anything that you want to add to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm aware of the happenings during the Second World War in Yugoslavia, and I think apart from -- from the figures you named to which I do not directly agree, I think we should all or could all agree that what happened at the time in Yugoslavia was a very bitter civil war apart from the policies of the German occupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you qualify it as a genocide, what happened to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly think there were genocidal attacks to the Serbs during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. David Owen testified here, and in his book The Balkan Odyssey, he also mentions, and I quote from his book, saying that, "The Nazis supported the creation of the independent state of Croatia, which included Bosnia and Herzegovina." I assume this is something you know. "Divided into German, Italian spheres of influence with the Croatian Ustasha Pavelic as a puppet ruler. During the following few years, his followers have committed unheard-of atrocities. Nuremberg referred and confirmed this as being genocide." And on page 106 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The witness must have a proper chance to answer these questions. Yes. Just a moment. Let the witness have time. Dr. Zwaan, if you'd like to respond to what's being put about Dr. -- the doctor's speech which was referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I have just said already, it's very clear that there have been genocidal attacks on different groups of population in Yugoslavia during the Second World War and especially on the Serbs, and it's well known that the Ustasha regime was set up by the Germans and also could stay in power as long as the Germans could stay in power and the Serbs or groups of Serbs have been victims of that regime is also a well known fact. I have nothing to add to that. But I may be, if you permit, I have not been writing about this in the report which we are discussing here, but I'm quite willing to try to answer questions, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is what I'm asking you, Mr. Zwaan. Since Lord Owen in his book is quite explicit, as is Simon Weisenthal. Lord Owen says on page 103, paragraph 3, and I quote: "The Croatian Ustashas in the Second World War committed genocide..." "The Croatian Ustashas in the Second World War committed genocide against the Serbs." I'm repeating for the benefit of the interpreters. I assume you read that book and that as an expert on genocide this statement must have been of interest to you.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not disagree with what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Doctor, what are, in your mind, the features of the killings of the Serbs in the Second World War that allow you to qualify them as genocide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, that's a very complex question, because of all the Serbs who were killed during the Second World War there were killings from different sides by different armed forces. But I think the situations in which Croatian troops and also German troops have killed large groups of Serbian, defenseless civilians would qualify as genocidal crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the numbers killed, you said you didn't agree with the numbers killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with the number of 600.000 Serbians killed during the Second World War. It's generally, in historical and sociological sources about the Second World War the total amount of victims in the whole of Yugoslavia is usually put at about 1 million, of which about 300.000 were killed in Bosnia, and it's very hard to say how many people were killed, for instance, in the camp of Jasenovac because there were no precise administrations made of the people killed. But as far as I know, the best experts estimate the amount of Serbs killed between 100.000 and 120.000. Killed in genocidal violence, that is to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How important are the numbers to you in arriving at your conclusion? You say the numbers were 10.000. Would that make any difference? Or is there something that's more important than the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's also quite a difficult question. It's usual to talk in statistical terms, but I think it's at least as important to look at specific individuals and peoples, people who were killed, and in that sense I wouldn't give too much importance to the exact numbers, but I would also underline that even if a few thousand people, defenseless people, were deliberately killed by armed forces, I would consider that a very serious thing. That's about what I think about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'd agree it's a serious thing, but whether as a sociologist you would characterise it as genocide is another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a form of genocidal attack, certainly. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zwaan, you are obviously among those people who are minimising the scale of the genocide of the Serbs. Do you know that a key scientific concern --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. If you're going to make that sort of allegation to a scholar of this sort, you must give the witness a chance to answer. Yes, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm certainly not minimising nor maximising anything. I'd like to point out here in a general sense that the numbers or the figures of people killed in genocidal acts are usually very much contested by different groups later on, which might be perpetrators but also victims and also outsiders. So in most cases it's very difficult to ascertain with a certain measure of reliability the total amount of people killed in certain situations. That's a very general problem which happens all the time. And there are people profiting from minimising these numbers, and there are people profiting from maximising these numbers. And scholars, I think we should be very skeptical about the parading of all sorts of numbers and we should try as best as we can to come to more reliable estimates, and that's what I'm trying, not more, not less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you have explained that it is possible that people profit from large figures or small figures, I have quoted the data from the Simon Weisenthal Centre with reference to the Serbs, not the Jews, although its main concern was the genocide of the Jews. Do you believe that Simon Weisenthal Centre is profiting if they say that 600.000 Serbs were killed in those camps and throughout Croatia, and when describing the Ustashas he says 500.000 killed, 250.000 expelled, and 250.000 converted to Catholicism. What kind of profiting can we talk about when referring to the Weisenthal Centre?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be something you have to research at the Weisenthal Centre, and you should ask there which people are responsible for what reasons for giving these numbers. I don't know, but I do not agree with these numbers. That's all I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they have been studying the issue since the Second World War to the present. As far as I understand it, however, you have been studying this for only a few years. Do you consider yourself to be more Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. competent than this centre for questions of genocide or not? Or do you believe them to be more competent?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see no sense in answering this question, because these are not matters of competence so much but matters of arguments, and as far as I know, the best experts on the total amount of victims during the Second World War in the Balkans usually use more reduced estimates. I have no judgement whatsoever on the comparative competence of myself and/or the Weisenthal Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that there were pronounced efforts even on the part of the former Croatian president, Franjo Tudjman, who was a historian, by the way, and whose aim was to minimise the crimes of the independent state of Croatia, especially in his book, his well-known book The Historical Truth.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the book by Mr. Tudjman. As far as I know, it has been reviewed in the professional press as not competent at all, because Mr. Tudjman was not only a military historian, or boasted as such, but he was first and foremost a Croatian nationalist politician. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Zwaan, since you specialised in genocide, especially with reference to the Jews, you aware of the alliance of the Jerusalem Muftija with Hitler, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Present-day Bosnia-Herzegovina was a part of Pavelic's independent state of Croatia. You're aware of that, too, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I want to add that probably not the population was asked whether they wanted to be part of that government, yes or no. They were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that Alija Izetbegovic, too, has a past link to genocide?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for your arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As an argument, I will read a brief quotation from a book by the Belgian Michel Collon entitled, Poker Menteur - Les grandes puissances la Yugoslavie et les prochaines guerres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before you do -- before you -- let's hear who this man is, if the witness can accept it. Do you know this gentleman whose given the evidence he wants to quote from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've heard his name, but I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So a very brief quotation from this book. It is an edition of 1998, page 268 to 270. "Born in 1925, the young Izetbegovic before the war," and the reference is to the Second World War, "...was active among the young Muslims, a traditionalist group fighting against deviations into modernist Islam, a fundamentalist organisation from the very onset. In the spring of 1943, Izetbegovic headed the Muslim youth in Sarajevo, and in that capacity he included Amin El-Husseini, the great Muftija from Jerusalem who fled to Germany and who was a friend of Hitler's. The mufti urged a jihad, a holy war against the Jews. Upon his call, 20.000 Bosnian Muslims were engaged within the Waffen SS. Izetbegovic was one of the organisers of the creation of the well known --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must bring this to a pause, to a period which can be answered. As to the doctor as to whether he could comment about any of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what I do say is maybe is that the mufti of Jerusalem was a rather eccentric personality who was one of the very great exceptions in the Islamic world at the time felt for a close alliance with Nazi Germany and was strongly anti-Semitic, but at that time anti-Semitism was not widespread in the Islamic world, nor among common Islam believers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The point of what I read out was that 20.000 Bosnian Muslims were engaged within the Waffen SS, and Izetbegovic was one of the organisers of the creation of the well-known SS Handzar Division. These Muslim SS members committed such atrocities toward the Serbs that even German officers were shocked. And this division would later be withdrawn from the Bosnian front and be sent to fight against the SSSR, against the Soviet Union. Are you aware of this fact? I'm not just talking about the eccentricities of the mufti but about the formation of this Handzar Division consisting of Bosnian Muslims and the cruelty and brutality that shocked even the German officers that they applied against the Serbs. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certainly aware of several of the facts, although I would phrase them probably differently. But if I may add to that a general command, if you allow me. You have been discussing now genocidal practices and intents of Croatians in history and also of Bosnian Muslims in history, but if I may quote yourself, you were talking just a few minutes ago about the dirt in front of your own door. Maybe we should discuss that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as our own door is concerned, I can say with pride that in Serbia, which I was the president and in which in addition to Serbs as the majority people, there were 27 other ethnicities living there throughout the Yugoslav crisis and not by a fraction has the composition of the population changed nor has anyone been discriminated against. So that as far as Serbia is concerned, it has really nothing to clean in front of its own door. But let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Before you go on, the witness must have an opportunity to answer. Is there anything you would like to add, Doctor, to what's been said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I have anything to add by what has just been said by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zwaan, you must know, though this is a minor detail, that in 1946, Izetbegovic was sentenced for nationalism and Islamism, and in 1970, he published in Sarajevo his well-known Islamic declaration presenting the gist of his views. I assume that you did have occasion to familiarise yourself with this book, and I'm again quoting Michel Collon when he draws attention to this, and this is contained in Izetbegovic's declaration when he says that, "The Islamic movement can and should take over power as soon as it is strong enough morally and numerically, not only to topple the existing non-Islamic authority but to be able to build a new Islamic authority. In those days, the Tito regime tolerated this, endeavouring to establish good relationships with the Arab countries. However, 13 years later, Izetbegovic was sentenced to 13 years in prison because of Muslim nationalism which endeavoured to create an ethnically pure Islamic state in Bosnia." And as reported by Le Monde in August 1993, Animam [phoen] was sentenced because he wanted to abolish mixed marriages. Briefly this is a lengthy career characterised by fundamentalist racism. Are you aware of these facts stated by Collon and the sources that he refers to?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to react to two points in your rather long declaration. In 1946, as you probably well know, and also the years thereafter, tens of thousands of Yugoslavians were sentenced to prison sentences, and many were executed for many different reasons by the Tito regime. These included so-called fascist collaborators, nationalists, fundamentalists, Islamists, and so forth and so on. So in that sense, I do not think that the sentence which was incurred by Mr. Izetbegovic is in any way a very special thing. The second thing I would like to point out is that to my knowledge, Mr. Izetbegovic, never tried in any practical sense to realise a homogenous Islamic state. I at least know of no evidence of actions of his to realise such a thing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have enough time to go into more detailed explanations of this, but what was in fact happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina and especially bearing in mind his own statement about it to the effect that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Islamic movement should and can take over a power as soon as it is morally and numerically strong enough not only to be able to topple the existing non-Islamic authority but to build a new Islamic authority which he in fact endeavoured to do during the outbreak of the Yugoslav crisis and the break-up of Yugoslavia that had vast and tragic consequences. I assume that this must be sufficient argument for you, too, in support of this statement. Is that so, Mr. Zwaan, or not?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, that's not so. I would like to point out two things. Firstly, the Islamic minority in Yugoslavia is indeed a minority. It's an outrageous thought that such a minority would ever dare politically and/or military [sic] to take over a whole country in which they form a minority. That's one point. The second point I would like to add is that the government of Mr. Izetbegovic and other leaders tried for a long time to keep true to the principles of multi-ethnic and multi-cultural Yugoslavia in contrast to the central authorities of several different republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the accused asks his next question, I must observe that none of the questions so far have actually dealt with the subject matter of the evidence, namely the method by which genocidal crimes are committed. And of course if the accused doesn't challenge the evidence on that point, it will stand unchallenged and available to us to apply in argument to the facts charged against the accused. The second thing is that there comes a point when if the accused simply asks as if asking historical questions about whether this or that was a genocide when it will be appropriate, whether in re-examination or when the Chamber may think, or otherwise to ask what this witness's opinion may be of the very event that he has avoided for reasons of leaving the matter to the Judges. But it shouldn't be left -- I need say no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is not uncommon for this to happen in this trial. We are aware of it. The method which we use is to control the amount of time which is available to stop this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shall obviously come back to this in re-examination if the accused carries on attempting to characterise every other event as genocidal without focusing on what is actually at issue here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To some extent it's a matter for him, but first let me consider for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Dr. Zwaan, can I ask you this: You were asked some time ago by the accused whether you had in mind the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in producing the report, and you said no. Indeed, the -- the Prosecutor made it clear that that was not one of the matters that you were to take into account.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Nonetheless, I have to ask you whether that situation has not somehow influenced the character of your report, perhaps even at a subconscious level.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's very hard, Your Honour, to talk about my own subconscious. I cannot deny, however, that when you study a subject as a scholar, you try to do your utmost to -- to -- to relate to all the sorts of previous knowledge you have about different cases. So I cannot exclude reacting to your question that from time to time, I've also thought about things which happened in Yugoslavia, because I've written about Yugoslavia before, in the early 1990s and also halfway through the 1990s. So I know quite something about the history of the area and the society. So I cannot exclude that that may have been in my mind also, and also other cases of genocide and severe political crisis have been in my mind, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that the very thing which the Prosecutor asked you not to have in mind might somehow have -- have slipped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think -- I don't think -- if you permit me, I don't think you could put it that way. It's not -- it's not that you can say that this has slipped, because what is in your mind, as we all know, I think, is not something you're perfectly always continuously aware of, nor can you be asked and/or able to exclude certain parts of your knowledge from what -- from what you're writing actually at a certain point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So let me put it more frontally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're obviously aware of what happened in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And you know the features, the characteristics of that situation. And it would obviously diminish the quality of your report if your report were tailored somehow to -- to meet those characteristics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would put it far too far, to my mind. I'm not aware of any effort on my part to try to do that, as you just say, no. But I am aware of my knowledge of the Yugoslavian crisis and also several other cases which are just in my mind. So when I'm writing about the subject, it's more or less inevitable that I also think about that from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, before you go on, remember this: Your time is limited. You will not be stopped in your examination. It's a matter for you. But bear in mind there is already produced by the witness a report which is already before the Trial Chamber and before the Court. If you want to challenge that in the next half hour or so, then you must do that. If you don't examine, then of course the same considerations will be taken. It's up to you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in this connection and in connection with what Mr. Nice said a moment ago, that it was my duty to question a report like this -- and here we're dealing with efforts by Mr. Zwaan to give us a sociological explanation of the phenomenon of genocide, which took as its basis, Jews, Armenians, Cambodia, and Rwanda and have an academic discussion on the phenomenon of genocide. He asked me -- he said I should challenge that now. To bring forward an expert witness of this kind - because that is what this witness is - is yet another confirmation of my assertion that he is along the political and media lines and not in the legal sphere, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a matter for you to ask your questions within the proper limits. Now, let us go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to emphasise that precisely what Mr. Robinson has just said, that this is - how shall I put it? - was launched intentionally so that on this occasion mention should be made of some sort of genocide, because they have no legal arguments Then. What they're going to do is delve in publicist aspects, because this is a more publicist approach, rather than a scientific one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zwaan, in the introduction -- yes, I shall be dealing with the report, Mr. May. I'm doing so now. In paragraph 2 you say that "The purpose of this report is not to question the existing legal definition of genocide, nor is it to step outside its frameworks." I assume, Mr. Zwaan, that a -- when this legal definition is mentioned, you have in mind the one contained in the Convention on the prevention of the crime of genocide and punishing the perpetrators dated back to 1948 that was taken over in the statute of this so-called Tribunal and also taken on by the Rome court, the permanent International Court of Justice. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So your report in none of its parts analyses the legal definition of genocide then, which we are endeavouring, at least where Mr. Nice is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. concerned, to apply to concrete cases. On the contrary: From the report, we can see that its goal is not to analyse genocide from the legal aspects. So you're just quoting Article 2 of the 1948 Geneva Convention, and everything ends there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's right. What I did try to do are two things: I put forward in my report that there is a continuous discussion within history and social science about the meaning of the term "genocide," which is very complex and difficult. In that context, I also quoted the most widely known legal meaning of the concept of genocide, and that's why I quoted the Convention. But I did not have the object, as I state very clearly in my report, to get into any legal and/or juridical discussion about the concept, but I wanted to know what are accepted as general insights in the field of genocide studies about genocide. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is generally accepted what has been written down in the Convention itself, because if you are not dealing with those questions, how then do you think your report can assist any court of law in getting to know the elements of genocide and what it constitutes? Because any court of law, even one like this, which is an illegal one, is duty-bound to apply positive law and not to delve into somebody's theoretical concepts which have nothing to do with law. Is that clear to you, Mr. Zwaan?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not clear to me at all. I've never had any pretension of going into any legal discussion. I have been asked here to produce a general report which was -- which states the general historical and sociological aspects of genocide, and that's what I've tried to do as best as I can. And I hope to assist, thereby, to get some more clarification about a very difficult subject, but I do not pretend - let me say it again - to go into any legal definition and/or discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But I assume that you're not contesting that genocide is a crime, it is a criminal act, and therefore a legal category by the same token. I don't suppose you question that.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't question that, but I'm not focusing on it. Maybe I can say it in this way: I've tried to evade discussions about guilt in legal form. What is interesting to me as an historian or a sociologist is how such phenomena as genocide arise in certain societies under certain conditions. And that's what I try to understand. I'm not pointing at the guilt of certain persons and/or categories of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. You deal with the sociological aspects of the phenomenon, or at least that was your intention, to deal with the sociological aspects of the phenomenon itself. However, is the fact that you do not deal with and analyse literature dealing with the legal aspects of the phenomenon -- and there are a lot - there is a lot of that - isn't that an indicator that you nonetheless wish to step outside the frameworks of the Convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide or don't you know about all this rich legal literature that exists on the subject?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the existence of quite a formidable legal literature on the subject, but I did not include that in any way into my report, nor did I comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Is that an indicator that what you wanted to step outside the frameworks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us not waste further time on this point. You've made your point. The witness has dealt with it. Now, just simply going over the same point endlessly is a waste of time. Now, if you've got any relevant questions, relevant, for this witness you can ask. Otherwise, it's a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zwaan, after quoting Article 2 of the Convention, in paragraphs 4 to 13 -- there seems to be some interference in the equipment. It's better now. Anyway, as I was saying, after quoting Article 2 of the Convention, in paragraphs 4 to 13 of your report, you speak about the dissatisfaction of different authors, usually not legal specialists, with the definition that the Genocide Convention provides, and you quote other proposed definitions for the crime of genocide. According to the authors that you refer to, the concept of genocide should be much broader than it is in the Convention and in other acts and legal documents which were -- which took over definitions from the Convention. Leo Kupar, for example, you talk about him in paragraphs 4 and 5, and others as well; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say that I quoted these different definitions to give the reader an insight into presently -- presently ongoing discussions within the field of genocide studies. It's also true, as you state, that some historians and social scientists have reflected on the pros and cons of the definition as given in the Convention, and I just try -- tried in my report to report just a small fraction of that discussion, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. It is obvious that behind you, just like behind Leo Kupar to whom you refer to in paragraph 5, the legal definition as you say in paragraph 5, and I'm quoting you: "Sometimes is too limited for historians -- is sometimes too limited for historians and social scientists who are trying understand and explain genocides and other mass crimes." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you happen to know from ancient times in law one of the most important principles was laid down, dura lexit lex?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Maybe you can explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A bad law is better than no law at all. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point of this, Mr. Milosevic? You want to make yet another -- yet another legal speech to a witness who is not answering in that way and has been told before we're not dealing with the law. Now, you're taking up a lot of time on a point which may have no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the point of this, Mr. Zwaan, is that law and laws must be respected, while -- until they are changed or amended through legal procedure. So do you know that the principle that I mentioned a moment ago is a basis for respect of the principles of legality, legal security and a series of other principles as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the witness wants to answer that, he can. Otherwise, it's nothing to do with him at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I can say two things. I'm not a lawyer, and I'm not discussing legal matters here. And the second point is I think you should realise, Mr. Milosevic, you are a lawyer, but there are different disciplines, like history and social sciences, and they operate on different principles than legal matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zwaan. Now, do you know that the provisions of the Convention which you mention, the one you mention, or to be more precise the most important of these provisions that you refer to, including a definition of Article 2, have outgrown the broadness of their application? Are you aware of that fact, that strengthens the position of the definitions contained in the Convention, and you say that the authors you quote are not satisfied with the definition?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me try and put it a different way. Do you know that the most important material provisions of the Convention have grown to become international customary law and that this was noted by the International Court of Justice with respect to the reservations on the Convention on the prevention and punishment, and it dates back to 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to have a discussion on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Zwaan, you can answer this evidence if Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you want to, this question which is being put, but it really may have absolutely nothing to do with you at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm very sorry, I don't think I have any answer to this. I am aware of the developments of international law, more or less, but again, I'm not a lawyer. Not discussing legal matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You hear that question, Mr. Milosevic. It's time you asked some questions which the witness can in fact deal with, instead of these other points which are your own interests. There is no point wasting your time with this witness and taking up your own time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Concentrate more on the phenomena of genocide, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but what I want to do is to clear one point up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the ruling of the International Court of Justice and their opinion, the opinions stated by them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not for this witness to deal with. You can produce it somewhere else if you want when you have a lawyer you want to talk to about it, or you can address us on it. There's no point wasting time with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. What the accused is trying to put seems to me this: Do you allow a possibility that you, as a socialist -- I'm sorry, I beg your pardon, as a sociologist, that can regard a certain phenomenon which cannot be defined as a genocide under the Convention as genocide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If -- if I -- I got what you're -- you're asking, I would give -- I would like to give an example. Under the Convention, the killing -- the large-scale killing of people who belong to the same ethnicity as the killers is not defined as genocide, and maybe I could give the example of the large-scale killings in Indonesia in 1965, which was done by Indonesian police and military personnel, and they were killing Indonesians and they were killing them because they thought or suspected them of being communists. Such a case would not be defined as genocide under the present Convention, and it has been argued by some historians and sociologists that in the longer run such cases should also be considered as genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, just to clarify one point, Mr. May. I started -- I broached the topic bearing in mind the fact that this expert witness brought in by Mr. Nice in his own paragraphs, paragraphs 4 to 13, speaks about the dissatisfaction on the part of various authors with respect to the definition contained in the Convention. And then I went on to explain that this dissatisfaction on their part and their line of thinking was completely irrelevant in view of the fact that the principles upon which the Convention is based is binding for all states, even in the absence of any contractual obligation because it has become part of international customary law, and therefore has been raised above the meaning and letter of the Convention itself. So it has become untouchable. And there dissatisfaction with the definition is quite irrelevant with that in mind. So that's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I understand you rightly, but I would like to observe that historians and social scientists are working in other traditions than lawyers and juridical specialists, and they're trying in other ways to understand and explain very complex social developments like, for instance, genocidal processes about which you're talking here. And historians and social scientists are not primarily preoccupied with legal matters but trying to understand, let's say, social and human and political matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I understand your academic curiosity and interest, because of course any subject can be discussed and debated, but we have very specific questions to deal with here, and I assume that you know that the rules emanating from the Convention, and you say that in their reports various authors were dissatisfied, have become part and parcel of customary law. And peremptory norms, that is to say part of what is called ius cogens, that is to say norms that cannot be derogated either by international covenants or national provisions and laws. They are on a higher hierarchical level and as such untouchable, and you as an expert for genocide, I assume, must know that. They are inviolable.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the question here is, but maybe I can clarify on one point. Many genocide scholars, historians and social scientists try to work with the generally accepted legal definition, but from time to time they find cases or they hit obstacles in their efforts to explain things with this definition. But Leo Kupar, for instance, and also Norman Naimark, and and also Eric Weitz, to name three very prominent scholars, have tried diligently to stay true to the definition of genocide as used in the Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But what about all this that I have mentioned, strengthening the position and raising them to a higher level of the most important provisions of the Convention, including Article 2 of the Convention, which you yourself refer to? Doesn't that indicate that from the legal point of view it becomes absolutely nonsensical to challenge the definition of the -- of genocide in the Convention and it's other important provisions because the stronger the position of these laws, the less there is any meaning to trying to challenge them. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me emphasise again that my report does not challenge in any way the existing legal definition. My only aim was to show that in history and social science discussions are going on about this very difficult concept of genocide. That's all I intended, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that is quite correct, Mr. Zwaan, because not only do the authors whom you quote question and challenge the definition governing the subject, but you yourself through in analysis in your report step outside what the Convention itself contains because in your sociological analyses you do not adhere to the legally established notion of genocide and the other provisions. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that is true. Let me emphasise again that my report, as I stated at the beginning of the report, is a historical and sociological report. It's not a legal study. It's not a legal or juridical report. And I think you should see the differences between different disciplines. There is no automatic hierarchy between disciplines whatsoever. So you should acknowledge that there are different approaches to the same problem apart from the legal approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Nonetheless, it would be of interest to me, Mr. Milosevic, if you were able to point to parts of the report which you say depart from the definition in Article 2, because the witness has said that he himself has not done so. He has -- he has pointed to authors who have had difficulties with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's precisely it, challenging this and endeavours to expand it before an organ that pretends that it is a court. And we can treat the question only in light of firmly established legal norms that have passed the test of time, regardless of what anybody might think of them. Because here we're having a sort of academic debate, if I can put it that way, looking at the ways in which this can be -- the definition can be changed, in a narrow sense or a broader sense, and you can see that throughout the report. It's not a terribly lengthy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But not to waste any more time, Mr. Zwaan let me ask you this: Part of your report, 14 -- paragraphs 14 to 17 is entitled war, civil war and genocide crimes, and in that section you make a distinction and comparison between genocide on the one hand and war and civil war on the other; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I tried to differentiate these phenomena from each other. At the same time, I've underlined that they very often hang together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is there any sense in the realm of sociology as the most general science governing -- about society or any other science for that matter to compare completely different categories, because war of any type and genocide are completely different categories and they are not comparable?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think I compared them. What I tried to do is to make clear how our common concepts of war, civil war, and genocide refer to different parts of the same social reality in a certain situation under certain conditions it a certain time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You also say, and I'm quoting you: "That military and civilian victims of war are not considered to be victims of genocide and that the same holds true when we're dealing with a civil war," and that is contained in paragraph 14. I assume I've quoted you correctly.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that when you have two opposing sides, parties, and when those parties are at war it is difficult, well nigh impossible to speak about genocide? This would emerge from what you yourself state.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult, but it is not impossible, because the distinguishing criterion is whether people are fighting each other and both sides are armed and also organised to use force or, as in the case of genocide, people are killed or otherwise attacked, while one side in the conflict is armed and organised and the other side is not armed nor organised to use force. And that's the differentiating criterion. At least that's what I tried to argue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn unless you want to ask something very quickly. We'll consider for the moment how much longer this examination should continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Having regard to the time which has been taken, Mr. Milosevic, you have another 20 minutes should you require it of this witness to add to your examination. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. 20 minutes you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zwaan, I will quote now just the last paragraph -- the last sentence of paragraph 14 in which you say: "Civil war implies a conflict accompanied by violence between two or more armed organised parties in a society which were before part of one and the same sovereign state. The American historian and sociologist Charles Tilly has characterised such a situation as a revolutionary situation or a situation of multiple sovereignty where before one sovereign state with one clear central monopoly on violence over the whole of the territory existed, there are now several armed parties within the same territory embroiled in contest over the state, each claiming its own monopoly on violence, while the previous central monopoly has been fragmented and disintegrated." And then you refer in the footnote to the source. And then the last sentence is of key significance, as far as I understand your report, and I quote: "A civil war may also lead to considerable numbers of casualties among the fighting forces of the parties involved, and may bring about many civilian deaths, either directly through acts of war, or through atrocities related to military action, but again, the victims are usually not considered, are not considered victims of genocide." Does that mean, Mr. Zwaan, that in a civil war, to the best of your understanding and in the way you address it in your report, as a rule there is no genocide?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that would be quite a wrong conclusion. It's very well possible that in the context of a civil war, at the same time genocidal acts may take place. And I would refer here again to the differentiation I made earlier between killing defenseless people who are not armed nor organised to use force by a party, maybe a party in a civil war which is armed and organised to use force. So that would be the difference. Casualties which result from fighting between two armed and organised parties are usually not considered victims of genocide, and that's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is what I was referring to, in fact, because you say that in the case of genocide as opposed to a civil war, one party, and I quote you: "Are the persecutors and organised to resort to force, whereas the victims and persecuted are disorganised for the use of force." This is in paragraph 15. End of quotation. Can it be inferred from that that in a situation of civil war when all parties are armed and are at conflict with one another, the pre-conditions for genocide do not exist?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think a very important difference you should make here is between combatants and non-combatants. In every civil war you will have armed groups fighting each other, but next to them you will have, in general, a common civilian population who is not actively taking part in the violence or the military fighting but is usually a victim of what happens to them by the armed forces. So that will be a very important difference to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can one infer from your report that in a civil war, similar to the one waged, for instance, in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the pre-conditions for genocide did not exist as all parties to the conflict did have military force?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again here that depends on how you would circumscribe the parties. If you would mean by that the armed forces of the different sides I could agree, but you should look also to the fate of people, and also females, children, elderly people, who are not armed and nor actively taking part in the military conflict. And if you focus on them, you might discover maybe acts of genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that the victims of genocide only sporadically resist. You say this in paragraph 15. And that resistance is regularly suppressed by the more powerful force. Can one infer from that that genocide -- that there is no genocide if the victims do have the necessary force to resist?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here again, I think you're being too imprecise. You have to look at the specific situation and then see whether the victims of the violence of others were armed and/or organised and/or had the opportunity to resist. And you will find very often in cases of genocide that they don't have that opportunity and that they are not armed. So it's rather easy for armed groups, for instance paramilitary groups or police or military personnel, to dominate the group of victims or potential victims of genocidal acts because they are armed and organised, and the common people who are the victims are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And does what you say mean that in situations when the parties are exchanging fire on a continuous basis and engaging in combat it is difficult to talk of genocide?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be difficult, but it still will be possible if you look precisely enough at the situation you're talking about, and then you might enable -- be enabled to see that while fighting is going on between different people, on the other hand, innocent people might be killed by one or the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that genocide is not a war or a civil war but a form of one-sided killing and the victims are unprotected and powerless. This is in paragraph 16. And helpless. Do you consider this to be a constituent element of the crime of genocide?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zwaan, in your report, you do not address, at least not adequately, one might even say that you do not address at all the subjective and objective aspect of the concept of genocide, what we referred to as mens rea and actus reus, that is the intent and the actual execution, and these are key elements of the concept of genocide. Why is that so in your report, especially in view of the fact that the mentioned elements, though they are part of the legal concept of genocide, also have their psychological, sociological, and other definitions that are closer to your studies? So this is in response to your question, Mr. Robinson, where a case when the expert is deviating from the set concept. Because by not speaking about it, you are not speaking about genocide as it is defined in this Convention. Isn't that so, Mr. Zwaan?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think you get me quite wrong. Although I do not use the words "subjective" and "objective," I have certainly paid attention to the phenomenon you're referring to. For instance, by pointing out that there is a difference between individual motivations of perpetrators to participate in genocidal acts and a general sense of direction, purpose, and intent which may be imparted by a certain ideology, for instance extreme racist nationalism. So I do think that I made that difference without, however, using the words "subjective" and "objective," which I do not think are very sensible concepts in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this subjective element, that is the intent to destroy a group, isn't it a key differencia specifica, the basic distinguishing element of genocide as opposed to other forms of violence? Of course not war because these are phenomenon of a completely different nature and character, which are simply incomparable. Would you agree, Mr. Zwaan, or not?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I get your question, but I would think that the intent to destroy a group, which might mean quite a few things apart from direct killing, but that the intent to destroy a group is certainly a distinguishing element of genocide. Yes, I would agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 27, in the part under the heading political leadership and the crime of genocide, you say that a decisive influence over the political decisions of the political authorities of the central level can be formulated in various ways. Some authors, like Chalk and Jonassohn, as well as Horowitz, talk about genocide by a state or other or by a state bureaucratic apparatus. As Helen Fein says, and you quote her, "Virtually everyone acknowledges that genocide is primarily a crime of [a] state. Others, however, prefer to speak in this context of the ruling elite, the political elite, the political establishment, (governmental and non-governmental) or the political leadership." If I understand you well, you have included in your report these references to confirm your thesis on the role of the state and the political elite in the time of genocide; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only my thesis. It's a general opinion in the field I'm part of, that genocide is virtually always a crime of state and then you can phrase that in different ways, and some authors, as I have tried to show, will put the accent on the state as an institution, while other authors will focus on the fact that the state is run by people, by certain political elites, who might use the state for their own political ends. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Proceeding from these quotations in your report, several questions come to my mind. First, is genocide committed by a group or individuals, members of a group, or is it a state crime as Helen Fein says that you quote?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's a very sensible form of differentiation. Individuals, as you well know, are always part of groups, and groups, as you well know, consist of individuals. So there is no sense here in making any strong differentiation between these two things, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A second question that comes to my mind is, to use your own terminology, members of a group that have a lower level of political power, can they commit genocide or is it a crime reserved for the political elite?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here again, I would like to point out that perpetrators of genocide are -- have to be differentiated. You have top-level decision-makers, you have sub-top-level or middle-level functionaries and commanders and you have lower-level personnel, and all these different layers in the hierarchy are in one way or another involved when it comes to genocidal acts. That's what I wanted to explain, tried to argue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but they are all, as you say here, are part of a certain hierarchy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That hierarchy might be more formal or more informal. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My next question has to do with the previous references to what you call state crime. Are you aware of the principle of individual criminal responsibility which is the fundamental principle of criminal law?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you also aware that the Convention on the prevention and punishment adopted that principle? I am referring to the Genocide Convention. It adopted that principle. It couldn't do otherwise, could it?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Although you might think that there are also other ways to think about these phenomena apart from individual responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Convention mentions all the possible perpetrators from those at the highest level to the lowest ones, and it clearly states that the commission of genocide is not reserved for the elite, as you say, or people in power, but that it may be perpetrated by ordinary individuals.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never stated that the commitment of genocide was reserved to political elite. I want to deny that very clearly. What I tried to point out is that during genocidal processes you have to deal with political elites who make certain decisions to launch such processes. Apart from that you have to deal with the hierarchy of the people who are involved in the actual implementation and carrying out of such grounds. That's what I wanted to underline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zwaan. Tell me, please, since you use those four examples, the Turks and Armenians, the Jews, Cambodia, and Rwanda, was each of these cases or generally when talking about the phenomenon of genocide throughout history, was each of those specific or did all cases of genocide resemble one another? Namely, do you not agree that the circumstances under which the Armenians and the Jews were persecuted contained numerous elements which could not be found in other cases?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you partly in the following sense: I think that every case of genocide has to be studied in its own specifics. That's one side of my argument. The other side, however, is that we are not using the word "genocide" for nothing. It means that we believe that there are phenomena which we can group under a certain common concept, genocide, and that we may study them comparatively in the hope, at least as intellectuals, to understand a bit more about the general conditions which lead to such situations and phenomena. Maybe I could give an example. If you use the concept of state, you think about certain general characteristics. On the other hand, you know very well that the present world contains nearly 200 states who are all different. Nevertheless, we use that general concept. And I think the same thing is at order when you talk about genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have two minutes left, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to make the best of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 19, there is something that I must admit I don't understand, and I would like to ask you to explain. You say: "Naturally, conditions of war and civil war may contribute strongly to the development of such crises," which means that war produces a crisis. I was of the conviction and still am that a crisis produces war, generates war. What is your opinion, please?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
