utterances.text: Well, I don't think you should lose yourself in wordplay here. A crisis could be defined, in a very general sense, as a fundamental destabilisation of a certain society. War may contribute to that. It might be a symptom of the crisis. It might also be that the war follows from the crisis, but it's certain for me that the situation of war is also a crisis in itself. Maybe I should leave it at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As I only have another minute yet, I assume two brief questions. Do you consider your report to be a fundamental analysis and identification of circumstances, at least from the sociological point of view, as you say in the introduction, that can lead to genocide? This is what you say in your first sentence. Do you consider your report to be a thorough study identifying the circumstances which can lead to genocide?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've certainly tried to write my report to the best of my ability, to explain what genocide is about and under which conditions it might or has taken place, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And in paragraph 24, you say, and I quote: "It is still not -- it has still not been specified which factors and causal elements are decisive for the emergence of genocide and other mass crimes directed against specific groups." In connection with this quotation, my question is to what extent you consider your report to be incomplete, because you yourself emphasise what I just quoted.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're quoting me quite out of context. If you would have read the report, you would have realised that what I say there has a relationship appearing to what has been preceding, but then in the next paragraphs and continuing in the report I try to outline the conditions as best as I can. So you're misquoting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The amicus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a point of explanation. I didn't misquote you. I quoted every single word that is found in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the amicus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Professor Zwaan, I want you to look at, first of all, about the disintegration and fragmentation of a state, and would you agree with this proposition, that when there is a disintegration and fragmentation of a state, what happens is that that causes the disintegration and fragmentation of that state's monopoly of violence, if it's accompanied by the formation of newly independent states who acquire their own monopolies of violence?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what you have there in that particular scenario of disintegration and fragmentation is a -- a complex process in the relationships between the parties.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The disintegration and fragmentation may have been purposefully launched in the break-up of that state.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. In most cases you should presuppose that there are parties at work who aim deliberately at the disintegration of the state, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's how it comes about. That's how the state fragments and disintegrates, because interested parties seek to pursue their own agendas in a different form to that which previously bound them to the main state.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be the case, although you must remember that there may be causes of disintegration from outside forces, other states trying to invade a territory and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's a further dynamic you can put into the picture that external influences --

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- may also cause that disintegration and fragmentation.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree with this: That once such a process is launched, it can quickly acquire its own unintended dynamics, which are then no longer completely controlled by any of the parties involved?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're quoting me, so I agree, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And which may subsequently carry along all parties towards an uncertain future and outcome?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is usually the case in situations of war and civil war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which means that the fragmentation and the disintegration which initially occurred, which had been put into a process that had been launched, that unintended dynamics from the launch of that process may occur that mean that the situation is no longer completely controlled by the original parties involved.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree to that, but I would emphasise the word "completely." It's no longer completely controlled, but it might be very well partly controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's a matter of degree.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And once launched in that way, it may subsequently carry along all parties towards an uncertain future and outcome?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That has been called the tragedy of history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And once launched in that way, it may not be foreseen how these events are going to unfold in the future, what may exactly happen.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody can look into the future. People can make conjectures but they can't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Fragmentation of the monopolies of violence are not controlled according to the old social controls.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Social, political controls. They're not controlled by the state in the same way that it previously exerted its control.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Although I would like to emphasise that you have to think in different phases. There might be a phase of disintegration followed by a phase in which new monopolies become visible and operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And that's where it creates its own -- it may create its own unintended dynamics.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And comes out of the control or completely out of the control of the parties originally involved.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parties will do their best to steer their own cause and control the processes as best they can, but maybe they are not succeeding in doing so, or only partly succeeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That process that we have been considering and looking at, as you say, comes from words that you have written previously is a description that you would be prepared to stand by as to what would happen in the disintegration and fragmentation of a state?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's your question precisely? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What we've been discussing you would stand by --

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- in your description of events that may occur in the disintegration --

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- and fragmentation of a state?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would stand by that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to deal with other -- one other matter, and that's at paragraph 16 of the report. It was touched on by Mr. Milosevic during his questioning of you, and it may be there's a passage of that that should be looked at as well in its full context. It might be helpful. I'm looking at the second sentence in paragraph 16. "Genocide is not war, nor civil war, it is a form of one-sided, not two- or more-sided, killing; the victims are essentially defenseless and helpless against the power of the perpetrators ..." We know the rest of the text there. It's not two- or more-sided killing. Perhaps you can explain what you meant?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to emphasise that in genocidal situations, whether they are about actual killing or other forms of trying to destruct people or the lives of people, that you have to deal with one party which is dominant, the perpetrators, the persecutors who are armed and organised and the other party is not. That's the difference I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Two- or more-sided killing" meaning?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can have a conflict with two parties. You can also have a conflict with six parties. I mean, civil wars may be very complicated if you look at the actual warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Several matters, but first you've been asked by the accused for most of the questions about your report on the basis that you're concerned only with genocide. The title of the report is "Genocide and Other Mass Crimes Targeting Specific Groups".

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And is your report and your conclusions concerned with characteristics of and conclusions that can be drawn when characteristics are found that relate to events that may be described as genocides but are more generally crimes that target specific groups?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I certainly think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to some of those characteristics a little later. His Honour Judge Robinson asked you if you'd in any way tailored your report by omitting expressly reference to or consideration of Bosnia and what happened there. We'll come to the reason for your exclusion of Bosnia in a second, but is there any question of your tailoring your report to lead to conclusions about Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not, to the best of my awareness, tailored anything in advance in any direction. I've just tried to write as best as I can, to the best of my knowledge, what I consider to be the main problems if you look at the phenomenon of genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tailoring, were it ever to happen consciously or subconsciously, would be writing a report that lent towards characteristics found in one setting that aren't found in another. Without going into it in any detail, just answer this please, if you can: Is there, in fact, anything in consideration of the Bosnian situation that is eccentric to and different from and would lead to different expressions of conclusion from the other events that you have considered?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that should depend on further study of the specific case. I tried to bring forward several tools of analysis by reference to which you might try to understand the certain specific situation. For instance, in Bosnia, but that would mean that that would have to be done, and I didn't do that in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And you didn't do it for the reason that we've given or you've given at the beginning of the report on instructions from the OTP, namely that of course the final question in these matters is always for the Judges; correct?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it also the case, of course, to consider that the Judges have evidence that is simply not available to you in its quantity and sometimes at all because it's evidence in private session?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's completely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that's -- those are included in the reasons why your report's been prepared in the way it has?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused spent time arguing or asking you about other genocides committed in the Balkans by groups and individuals but never by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You refer to, in your report, when looking at the way these crimes may be motivated, at the collective memory, its use and abuse.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there anything further that should be drawn to our attention about the comparison that the accused is now making between genocides and similar crimes he attributes to the others while saying that the Serbs have nothing to be blamed for?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that conclusion would be quite wrong. If I may only point to one example. The partisan army of Marshal Tito in 1945, 1946 supposedly, and there were many Serbs involved there, supposedly killed rather large groups of Croatian Ustasha fighters and also Chetnik Serbian fighters. So we didn't go into it but I think -- and I want to emphasise that all groups in the Balkans have a very tragic history, namely that they have been victims and also often perpetrators of large-scale violent crimes in their history, and they remember that. That's part of the collective memory of people. And has been pointed out by other scholars you very often seen in cases of genocidal acts that you have to deal with repeat offenders, or that it happens again and again. And if you look at the Balkan wars and the First World War and the Second World War and the recent conflict in Yugoslavia, you see that memories of the past are continuously active in the new rounds of conflict. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, did the late President Tudjman ever allege reciprocity of genocide?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- would you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Did the late President Tudjman ever allege reciprocity of genocide as between Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge -- I'm not quite sure here what you mean by reciprocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it only ever alleged by the Serbs that they were victims or was it also alleged by the other side that they were victims?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tragic thing is that most nationalist leaders in the Balkans tend to see themselves as victims and the others as perpetrators, and there is a very great lack of disposition to acknowledge any guilt in the historical process and that also has to do with the great lack of freedom under communism in the Yugoslavia. So the recent past of the Second World War was never discussed extensively scientifically and intellectually in a sufficient sense. So these old memories, which are partly truth and partly myth, have never been dismantled, so to speak, by serious research and serious open discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made a reference in answer to an observation or a question by the accused to the dirt in front of the door. In the questions he subsequently raised with you, has he ever dealt with that topic?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Robinson queried with you the significance of numbers killed when the accused was proposing numbers in the Second World War killed larger than you would accept. Is maximising numbers a feature of reliance on collective memory when motivating crimes of this kind?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very often the case, although I would also like to underline that there is real tragedy in the past of the Serbian people in this case that they have been victims of genocidal attacks. So there is some historical ground for Serbian people to see themselves as victims of the aggression of others, but this is also the case for Croatians and for Albanians and for many other groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay asked you some questions about the disintegration of state and then went to the conclusion that further events may be unforeseen. I think two or three points. If a state or a republic or a federal republic disintegrates in a way that its component parts become separated and recognised, do those component parts and the governments of them then owe a duty properly to control the new monopoly of violence?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly have that duty, yes, to my mind, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Once the duty exists and the state is recognised, is interference with that monopoly of violence from inside or outside one of the characteristics of this type of crime that you might look for?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should certainly look at such events if they are there as pre-conditions for genocidal crimes, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we'll come back to one or two of the ways in which your report deals with that later. But staying with Mr. Kay's question, it seems to be suggesting or allowing for the responsibility that in the unforeseen events of a disintegrating state, mass killings -- or this may be what it is directed at, mass killings of innocent people or mass expulsions of innocent people, unarmed, perhaps, is a natural phenomenon. You said in your report that this type of crime and event is not a natural phenomenon. Are you accepting that simply in the unforeseen events of a disintegrating state the mass killing of innocent people suddenly becomes a natural phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not. And I must also point to the example maybe of the break-up of Czechoslovakia which happened in a peaceful way by dealings between political elites from both sides. And I could also point in the case of Yugoslavia to the secession of Slovenia, which did not lead to large-scale killing. About 60 to 70 people were killed in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that in your analysis if -- following a disintegrated state one finds, for example, mass killings or mass expulsions, does one look still for the same characteristics to see if we're dealing with this type of crime, genocide or similar?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. You should study every case in its own context and then decide whether the one phenomenon or the other is occurring and try to explain why it does occur. At least that's as an historian or sociologist I would try.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Mr. Kay also asked you about one-sided killing. I think you told me yesterday, is it possible for these crimes to be occurring within a multi-sided conflict just harder sometimes to isolate the material showing their existence?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I don't think so. It might be more -- it will be more complicated if you study a more-sided conflict, because you have to dispose of quite large amounts of more or less reliable facts. But it is not in principle more difficult than when you have to deal with two sides to a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple of particular questions. One general topic and then I'm done. There was a debate, a discussion about the necessity or apparently the necessity for victims of genocides to be armed. Is it in fact possible for these crimes, genocidal crimes, to be committed against armed people, indeed against combatants?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I mean, when people get killed in genocidal acts, they are mostly in all cases unarmed. And if they are armed, and I could give you an example, they will be disarmed before they will be killed. And I could give the example of Armenian officers and soldiers in the Ottoman army at the beginning of 1915, who were called to the ranks in relationship to the First World War, but when the Ottoman leadership, or the Turkish leadership, I should say, at the time decided to launch a genocidal campaign against the Armenians, all these officers and soldiers were dismissed from the ranks, they were disarmed, and they were organised in so-called labour battalions which were mostly worked to death frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to ask you about another example. Would the uprising of the Jews in the Warsaw ghetto, thus they not being armed necessarily save that circumstance from characterised as genocide by sociologists or historians, whatever might be the position in law.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I certainly don't think so. I think you should realise that that revolt in the Warsaw ghetto was a revolt of very young people who had postponed their actions until nearly all the Jews already from Warsaw had been transported Treblinka, so only a small number of Jews was remaining behind, and at that time it was more or less desperate effort, also impossible to win, to put up resist answer against an overpowerful destructive enemy, the German army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then finally, the accused in his questions about war and civil war -- or first of all, just this, as between war, civil war, and genocide, is it ever the case in your experience that leaders mask or seek to mask the reality of genocidal-type crimes by assertion that it is war only?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very often the case, yes. And it's still the case, for instance -- for instance, the present Turkish government, which is still arguing that the Armenians were not killed by genocide but by war actions. Just one example, but I could give you many more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused asserted that the pre-conditions for this type of crime did not exist in the territory with which we are immediately concerned. Your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a last -- that is not the case. They did exist, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the accused hasn't dealt with the detailed characteristics that you've identified, but do they include, for example, things like the impunity that may be accorded to paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be a very important consideration here, to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A progressive event?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Something that only comes to be stopped by outside intervention?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sustained for its duration by propaganda?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's very often usually the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, Dr. Zwaan. You were asked by Mr. Nice in reference to the -- a question by the accused that the accused said that the pre-conditions for this type of crime did not exist in the territory with which we are immediately concerned, that being Bosnia, and you answered, yes, they did exist, but then I recall that you said that you did not concentrate on the circumstances in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your report doesn't deal with Bosnia and Herzegovina, but here you're giving an answer that relates specifically to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you well, I see no contradiction here. I have been asked as well by Mr. Milosevic as by Mr. Nice more than one question about the situation in Bosnia, and I've tried to answer them as best as I can, but that does not mean that I've written my report with Bosnia in mind. On the contrary. Is that sufficient answer to your question, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as indeed the Court will remember as I explained this a couple of days ago, the writings of the witness in relation to the former Yugoslavia, insofar as they've been summarised in an English language version, were provided as a matter of courtesy to the accused and to the amicus so that they could know what his overall position was in case there was anything that he said that they wanted to contradict him with. Your Honour, I haven't formally moved the report into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That should be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 639, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Zwaan, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence. We thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the curriculum vitae for Dr. Zwaan will be 640.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Inevitably, as we reach the closing of this stage of case, there will be administrative difficulties, and I think it's better that I outline some of them now before I call the next witness, to both inform the Chamber and the parties because it affects the order of witnesses and in certain cases to seek relief. I can deal with it mostly in open session and using pseudonyms where appropriate. The witness for today is ready, and I think tomorrow the probabilities are that we are going to be taking the witness Manning whose material is ready and has been served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt so we can make sure we have the record. How long do you anticipate the Prosecution will be with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I imagine one session. I hope not longer. The equivalent of one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But then he will obviously be some time in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll try to take him as shortly as I can because he's been partly 89(F)'d and because of the desirability of being brief. But yes, he will be some time in cross-examination I forecast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then Manning to follow tomorrow. Manning, of course being an in-house witness so he can be called on, and as it were, sent back or dealt with part whichever is most convenient to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pausing there and this witness is going to be some time or is bound to be. I notice that you refer to four hours. I'm not sure on what basis --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was much earlier and I think that was a time interval that slipped through earlier from the regimes of evidence in chief. I hope to be much less than that. I hope he will be much less than that. And I'm going to take only the matters that I think are truly valuable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have got a fairly lengthy document here in his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next week at the moment on Monday, B-235 is listed, living no names or other material detail, a lengthy statement from this witness has been provided in English but only the day before yesterday, and the B/C/S version will be provided only today. From that lengthy statement, only a small part is required. At the moment, the summary is 11 pages. It may reduce, but of course I recognise straight away for him to be taken on Monday, even only the few pages, would require leave to abbreviate time. We would ask you to consider that, and we'll get the abbreviated summary to you as soon as may be for you to consider that. If he is not to be taken on Monday, it may be that we can advance B-1804, who would otherwise come next or who would come next. His material has been served. An 89(F) statement will, I hope, be served today. I think now I should ask for private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's no other witness I think on your list, present list, for next week. If I can then -- and one of our problems is who to bring forward, if we can, to fill the gap. If the Court would look to -- I think it's probably on your list, the 5th of February, there's General Vegh. I think I've explained before that Hungarian General Vegh, whose report has been served, suffers from -- before I come to the circumstances of the witness, I should tell you that the Serb translation of his report is still not complete, one of the difficulties being the general overloading of CLSS and also their professional standard requirement such as footnotes are all provided to them in the original text. So they actually call for a lot of documents in order to check the accuracy of footnotes which is their standard and we don't gainsay it. But that's, I gather, the problem leading to the delay in the final provision of his served translation. We are seeking to get round that problem, but we can't be sure when the last part of his report will be available in B/C/S. Although I think it's been provided as it -- probably Friday as Ms. Dicklich tells me. You may not remember that General Vegh suffered catastrophic injuries in a road incident, and then after we'd retained him he suffered loss of hearing from which he has made a remarkable recovery by equipment that impresses everyone who sees it, but by reason of which he cannot fly. It's because of the inserts into his -- it doesn't matter why. Therefore, and experiments have been done and arrangements made for him to be dealt with by a videolink, but we haven't yet made the application because we weren't sure whether we would have time for him and we didn't know the date when he might finally be called. I think there's an outstanding administrative issue at the Hungarian end, but it is possible that those hurdles could be got round if the Court were favourably to view an application for videolink and that he could be accelerated into next week, maybe the 28th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I say this formally? There are a very, very large number of exhibits with which have been produced. I don't think you even know, if I can say bluntly, that you know how many you've put in, although you should. But the fact is that we need to keep this to an absolute minimum that we can deal with at the end. Otherwise it's putting too much on all those involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I'm acutely aware of that myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So if any can be reduced in any witnesses who come, they should be brought to an absolutely bare necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I couldn't agree more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The total figure should be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the total figure has been calculated. Whether there is a running total going but it was calculated in accordance with your instructions. So, Your Honour, there -- so the possibilities for next week and to which I will return obviously much more briefly but I'm setting out the whole difficulty now could be General Vegh. If it's not General Vegh, then we simply may not be able to fill those three days. We're doing our best, but there is that problem. And therefore, just to review it again, we would seek your indulgence as to the abbreviation of time in relation to B-235. We will seek your further guidance if it's appropriate for the following witness, and we may seek to accelerate General Vegh. Can I then go into private session for the next passage, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. You'll have your chance in a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let him finish. Let the Prosecution finish, and then you'll get your chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have finished save to remind myself that the witness Theunens, the military analyst expert might also be accelerated into next week if there's a gap, subject to the fact that only three-quarters of his materials have been translated into B/C/S at the last count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It really would be of assistance to have something in writing about this because of the number and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: -- Variation you want to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I gather that the rest of Mr. Theunens's report is available today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's important that everybody knows and it's important in particular that the accused knows what he is going to face at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely. So therefore to summarise it's the witness listed followed by Manning as time allows, then we hope B-235, then B-1804, and then possibly (redacted), possibly (redacted) for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. What do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have noted down the things that Mr. Nice has just referred to, the changes with regard to the list of witnesses. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- what Mr. Nice mentioned in closed session, I will also refer to that in closed session -- private session. Mr. Nice said just now that after this witness who is coming next that we will have Mr. Manning. I have received the material one might say on time, but the witness coming after that, Witness 235, I still haven't received any documents. It may be an error, but I wish to draw your attention to this. Furthermore, Mr. Nice said that he will be followed by B-1804, and according to my notes, he said that for 1804 the material would be served today. I have to protest once again that I must have some elementary information about somebody who is planning to appear already on Monday. You have repeatedly said that I should get those documents at least ten days in advance, and in this case not even that minimum term has been observed. Also, I heard you, Mr. May, explaining a moment ago which I believe is quite correct that in connection with this General Vegh, a large quantity of material has been disclosed. I don't have those documents. I don't have a schedule of witnesses in front of me, but I don't remember General Vegh being on that list. And now with reference to the documents that Mr. Nice spoke about 10 or 15 days ago, Mr. Nice said here that he had finally received from the Yugoslav authorities minutes from meetings of the Supreme Council of Defence, and he symbolically showed with his hand a pile of them, indicating that there was a big pile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have not as yet had the answer. We will mention it now since you raise it. Let me say about the other matters we have in mind the whole time that you should have the opportunity to deal with these matters in proper course. We have it in mind, and the Prosecution will produce their latest plan. But on that particular matter, perhaps you can tell us what the state of play is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the Supreme Defence Council document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the Supreme Defence Council documents, yes, the -- it's becoming clear that -- well, first of all, the accused has had a summary of them in English because they came with a filing. They are now only still available in B/C/S so far as the stenographic notes are concerned, although we have B/C/S and English versions of the minutes. I'm having the documents put together in a format which will enable each meeting to be dealt with separately so that the Chamber ultimately and everybody else will be able to go to a single tab and see the documentation for the particular meeting, although at the moment the English language version of the stenographic notes will not be available. My calculation yesterday, looking at the material, is that the material in English and in B/C/S, when finally composed, will be five files, so that one language or another will be about two and a half files of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When is it likely to be ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't give you a date for the completion of it, but it's being worked on immediately and I'll come back to that possibly at the end of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything else you want to add, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely in connection with what Mr. Nice just said. He explained some ten or 15 days ago that he has the minutes from the Supreme Defence Council. He's adding now they're in Serbian. Of course they're in Serbian, because they were made in Serbian. He said about 15 days ago that they were at the disposal of myself and the amici and Your Honours, and my associate tried to get hold of those minutes or, rather, copies of them, and he was told that he couldn't get them yet. Now we are told that they will consist of some five big binders. I really don't understand why I couldn't have been served a copy in the Serbian language ten or 15 days ago, or at least a day when they will consist of five binders. I don't need the English translation to review those minutes of the Supreme Defence Council, which will be tendered as customary in great haste and in enormous quantities. So please answer my question: How do you imagine that for a witness who is due to testify in ten days' time - and in the meantime there will be other witnesses - how can I read five big files of minutes from meetings of the Supreme Defence Council in order to be -- find certain relevant things, as you always say, to cross-examine the witnesses? And especially I think it is absolutely unfair for me not to have received those documents although Mr. Nice has had them for 15 days, and they exist in the Serbian language, and they could simply have been copied and handed to my associate who is present here, or at least could you give instructions for those documents to be handed to my associates today?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the accused reminds us that I said these documents were available. Of course at the time they weren't in the form that would have been most convenient. Ms. Dicklich, who I think has a good day-to-day working relationship with the accused, to whom she communicates in provision of documents and with his associates has no recollection of any request being made. However, she tells me that there is a project in hand to get them on a CD-ROM, computer disk, available for the accused today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we cannot go on this argument. You've heard what they are prepared to do, to do the best they can to assist on the matter, and you should have the opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But please, I cannot see a single reason explaining why I could not receive the copies of these minutes in the form that Mr. Nice has available to him. What does it mean they will be transferred to CD-ROM and they will give me that? They have those minutes. Please give them instructions to copy them and hand them over to me. This is no extravagant request. It's a normal request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The matter's being seen to. Now, we will adjourn now. It's time for a break, though rather early.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. One at a time. We've got two minutes flat. Yes, what's your final point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally, I wanted to make an objection in connection with the mention of a witness who he mentioned in private session, because I don't have any statement of that witness. And Mr. Nice is telling us that he will be appearing in ten days' time. I don't have the statement. I don't have anything about that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been through this, and you've heard what the position is about ensuring that there is the ability. Now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One matter. There is a filing by the Prosecution before the Trial Chamber dated 20th of January for leave to call another witness, C-63, who hasn't been mentioned this morning within this context, which perhaps the Trial Chamber ought to bear that in mind concerning this application, further new materials, new witness at this stage of the case, given the burden of the rest of the witnesses on the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that. Let us adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if the witness would take the usual documentation, please, which the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd take a seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a file of exhibits associated with this witness, most of the exhibits being produced by statement served under 89(F) of our Rules. May the binder be given a general exhibit number for us perhaps to review the status of any exhibits produced, whether for identification or otherwise at the end of the exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 641, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your full name, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Hrvoje Sarinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Sarinic, have you provided two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, respectively tabs 2 and 4, and are you satisfied that those two statements are correct subject to one or two corrections that we're going to deal with in live evidence today?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I confirm that I did make those two statements and that I abide by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 1 of our Exhibit 641 is a curriculum vitae of yours that I think you've seen approved and signed, revealing so far as material that has been a matter of public record, that in 1990 you were appointed first chef de cabinet to President Franjo Tudjman severing as his advisor between 1990 and 1998, holding various posts, and you've set out in the curriculum vitae that you were a chief of his office, Prime Minister, chief of the office of national security, and then in 1994 recalled to head his office becoming chief political advisor and a member of Croatia's national Security Council acting, between 1993 and 1994, as chief negotiator with the UN representatives and UNPROFOR. Operating as the President Tudjman's confidential envoy to this accused; correct?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In those circumstances, I trust the Chamber has the proofing summary that maps our way through the exercise of examination-in-chief, but what I will do in accordance with the Court's order is start with the first statement, which is tab 2 and deal with the parts of it that I must deal with in live evidence. Setting a context, your first statement, Mr. Sarinic, deals with a meeting on the 26 of the January, 1991, with which I needn't trouble you, but then moves to deal with the meeting in Karadjordjevo in March of 1991, a meeting organised through the chef de cabinet Milinovic of the accused's office organised in secrecy and happening on the 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The meeting at Karadjordjevo, did you spend some 10 to 15 minutes with the late President Tudjman and this accused. In the course of that, did Tudjman say something to the accused about the log revolution? If so, what?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was there for about ten minutes or so, as you said. I was with them. And during that period of time, President Tudjman told the accused that he was behind the log revolution and that, of course, did not benefit Croatian-Serb relationships which were actually the central issue in Yugoslavia. Having heard President Tudjman's statement, the accused disagreed, but he said significantly, "I believe that we can resolve all those problems." I personally had the impression and thought about it, and in view of what happened subsequently, it all seemed to indicate that this sentence of the accused related to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same -- at the same time, did the -- did Tudjman say something about the arming of Croatian Serbs, and if so, just in a sentence what was the accused's reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: President Tudjman said that Krajina was the Trojan horse of Serb politics in Croatia and that they could not prevail without the authorities headed by the accused supplying them and standing behind them. The accused denied that and said that he had nothing to do with it, that perhaps the JNA may be involved but that he had nothing to do with the JNA. And he absolutely rejected President Tudjman's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the two men spent about four hours alone together, between 3.30 and 4.30, and ended on the basis that they would meet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, paragraphs 6 and 7 are subject of correction; they are misplaced. They relate to the next meeting, and I'll come back to them at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 8, on the return was Tudjman optimistic because of the talks?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tudjman was highly optimistic, and he said that he believed that the problem would be resolved peacefully and that with the accused, he would be able to find a common way of dealing with the problem. He was highly optimistic. And I must say that I told the president that I didn't quite share his optimism because the accused always had his fingers crossed in his pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 30th of March, Goran Milinovic proposed a further meeting at Karadjordjevo but eventually the agreement was made that it should be in Tikves. Your statement deals with an intervening meeting on the 28th of March of 1991 when all six presidents met at a scheduled meeting in Split. But you only set out there what you were told by Tudjman about the meeting. On the 5th of April at another leadership meeting, according to your statement, paragraph 11, Tudjman said that a question of dividing Bosnia and Herzegovina had arisen and that the proportion of forces would be crucial there because Slovenes are leaving, and he said the Serbs want a Greater Serbia; correct? Just yes or no if that's right.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as you were concerned and perhaps just add this -- I beg your pardon. The discussion on the 5th of April, was it referring back to the earlier meeting?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: You mean the previous meeting in Karadjordjevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was mentioned, but very briefly, because that meeting was normally to have been secret, but a certain number of men in the leadership of Croatia knew about it, and President Tudjman felt it would be a good idea to mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 15th of April of 1991 was the day of the Tikves meeting?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, did they meet in private?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: First of all, you yourself said that the Serb side insisted on the other meeting to be held in Karadjordjevo as well, but President Tudjman refused because Karadjordjevo, for the Croatian public, had a bad connotation, because in 1971, the spring -- the Croatian spring was broken up there. So he wanted the second meeting to be held in Croatia, that is in Tikves. We agreed again on that meeting, that is the chef de cabinet of the accused and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Excuse my taking you swiftly through this material. We go back to paragraph 6 and 7 of your statement which you alerted us to that it misplaced by us there. It is in fact after this meeting that on the plane on the way back to Zagreb, the late President Tudjman showed you a piece of paper, and tell us about that and what he said about that.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: First of all, after Tikves, President Tudjman was far less optimistic than he was after Karadjordjevo. That is the first point. So as we left shortly after the meeting, in the plane he said to me, "Here is what Slobo," as he called him, "gave me." And I looked at this piece of paper. It was written in black ballpoint pen, and roughly it said the following, that the Muslims were a major evil. Actually, that one should be cautious about this so-called green, zelena transverzala, going from Turkey, Bulgaria, Western Macedonia, Kosovo and Sandzak, and that this was a major threat for Bosnia and also for peace in the area, that the Muslims had already hung a green flag on Mount Romanija, a mountain close to Sarajevo, and that they wanted an unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina in which they would rule, while the Croats and the Serbs would be minorities. I immediately returned this piece of paper to the president, and later on when we discussed it, he said, "Well, there's something in it."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he tell you where he got the piece of paper from?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: He told me, yes, that he had received it from the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Paragraph 13 of your statement before we move on to matters that we don't have to give evidence about live. You express a view about whether or not the two of them reached any form of agreement. Can you explain how you formed your view about that and what your view was as to whether they reached an agreement?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: There was no formal agreement. Had there been a formal agreement, then all those horrors that came afterwards would not have taken place. So I was just reflecting on this, on both presidents having their own ideas about Bosnia and the division of Bosnia. That is the truth. But I do not believe that a formal agreement was reached. As far as Bosnia is concerned, I can convey to you several positions held by both presidents with respect to Bosnia. President Tudjman, as an historian, was saying that Bosnia was a historical absurdity resulting from Turkish conquests in the fifteenth century. He said that it would be a good idea to thicken that thin slip of land in the south, and he also conveyed some other reflections of his regarding Bosnia. As for the accused, he told me during one of our meetings that he can tell me quite frankly that with Republika Srpska, he had resolved 90 per cent of the Serbian national question, just as President Tudjman had resolved the Croatian national question with Herceg-Bosna. I think I have formulated quite precisely what the accused said. And then on another occasion - this was, I think, in 1995 - I asked him, "President, why don't you recognise Bosnia?" And his reply was, "Which Bosnia? Whose Bosnia? What kind of Bosnia?" So he was absolutely denying the possibility of the existence of Bosnia. I have to add something here, and that is that, as opposed to what the accused stated, the Croatian authorities were the first to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were the first to send their ambassador. They supported the referendum on independence. They signed the Split declaration, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Though I do have to say, if I may, if Their Honours allow me to finish, that even though in his reflections, but not only in his reflections but also in his statements, President Tudjman did give thought to the division of Bosnia as I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your statement goes on to deal with a meeting on the 27th of August of 1991 at Brioni. It doesn't involve the accused and it being taken in writing. Paragraph 19 you deal with a meeting on the 8th of January, 1992, the Presidency of the Republic of Croatia, and again not involving the accused. We can deal with that in writing. And we come, therefore, to the meeting arranged on the 9th and 10th of November of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should have said that -- yes, tab 3. If you want to find the page references for what happened on the 8th of January meeting, the page references to guide you through the exhibit, if you want to find it, can be found in the proofing -- in the summary that's been served today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move then to a meeting on the 9th and 10th of November, 1993, a meeting held on the instructions of President Tudjman to see if the accused had changed his position on anything and to see what his attitude then was on reintegration of parts of Croatian occupied by the RSK. And between that period and the end of 1995, I think you actually met the accused on 13 occasions, is it, as the confidential envoy?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 12th of November of 1993, the first meeting, perhaps we'll deal with this really quite briefly. What did the accused tell you about forces of Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Well, he said that the Muslims were amassing their forces in Central Bosnia, that they were rallying their forces to move towards the sea, towards Neum. And although he always spoke a little derogatorily of their military abilities and capabilities, that was more or less what was said. I don't know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that's enough for the purposes of identifying the meeting, which is not critical to the evidence you're giving. But perhaps you could just deal with this: In the course of this meeting, did you ask him about Knin and about Baranja, and did he give you a reply saying what was the effect so far as he was concerned about the establishment of Republika Srpska in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Those are two questions. One has to do with the so-called RSK, and there the accused said that Knin, at all events, was a Croatian town and that he had no territorial pretensions on Knin. I told him at that point, I said, "Mr. Milosevic, very well. That's as far as Knin goes. But what about Baranja?" And I had in mind generally Eastern Slavonia when I said that, not just Baranja itself. And his reply -- or, rather, I said a little jokingly, "I would like to know what you have in mind with a view to Eastern Slavonia." And he said, "Well, if you were able to see what was in my head, you would have a pleasant surprise." So this remained a little mysterious, but that in general was the position taken at that time by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say anything about resolution of his problems by any of the bodies we've referred to? Or not his problems, Serbia's problems.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that that's what I said a moment ago, and that is that he told me, and that was towards the end of that particular meeting, that with Republika Srpska, he had solved 90 per cent of the Serb national question just as Tudjman had solved it with Herceg-Bosna, he had solved the Croatian national question. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: And then at the end of that same meeting, we discussed, and the tone was a little more leisurely, I asked him something about Arkan and his units, and laughingly the accused answered and said, "Well, I have to have someone as well who is going to do part of the job for me." So quite certainly without the support of an army like that which numbered 5.000 men, they couldn't have been supplied or armed or paid without having the accused stand behind it, because at the time the accused was all-powerful in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He said this, as you say, laughingly, but did you take it seriously? And if you want to qualify the way you took it, do so.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Well, I experienced it, and all of us who were there who knew about it experienced it as an expression used by the accused meaning that a skilful politician and a capable politician has to have people like that too. That's one side of the question. And on the other hand, we knew about everything that Arkan and his army had done, the evils they had committed. And we knew beforehand, before I actually asked the accused that question. And perhaps I asked the question for that reason. So we did know that the accused stood behind Arkan. And as the proverb says, there's always a little bit of truth in every joke. So although it was said laughingly, on a light note, I experienced it as being a reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I move to paragraph 28. In your early meetings with the accused, did the issue of Islamic fundamentalism arise? You've spoken of it already in relation to the piece of paper that the late President Tudjman had, but tell us about it, if it arose in these early meetings.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: I would say that that was the leitmotif of the accused generally. And he said to me on one occasion that there were about 2.500 Mujahedin who had come in from other Islamic countries to help their brethren in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he also told me that the Muslims are a great evil because of their demographic explosion and that it would all cost us a great deal unless we're cautious. So that this fundamentalism, and if we refer to the green tranverzala, the line I mentioned a moment ago, then this can be seen in very vivid form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 18th of January of 1994, to be particular, were you in Geneva with President Tudjman when at a meeting with the accused the accused touched on the demographic point in particular terms and also dealt with the media war or the media position?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend that meeting, and roughly speaking, if I can paraphrase what was said and recall the words that were said, I think the accused said that the Muslims are a great evil because of the great birth rate, the demographic explosion. And they have also won the media war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last two lines or three lines of paragraph 30 have already been covered by the witness. Paragraph 31 is in in writing. Paragraph 32. Did you speak to the accused after a first round of elections at which Babic had secured a narrow win?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did speak to him about that, and I joked with him a little because he stood behind Martic. And at that time, he said that Martic was the most capable man, et cetera, and I teased him a bit, because in the first round, Babic had won -- or, rather, let me say that a little before the elections took place, I said to the accused, "Well, I'm not sure that Martic will win, because Babic is backed by the Orthodox church." And his answer to me was, "Well, the Orthodox church isn't standing behind me and yet I am what I am." So that's the first point. And after the first round when Babic won, I teased him a little, as I say, and I said, "Well, your prognosis, your forecast don't seem to have been quite correct." And he said, "Yes, but I can see that there were some irregularities." "I hear there were some irregularities in the elections," rather, and after that the whole thing was declared null and void, and Martic was elected as president of that so-called RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did this show you, if anything, about the accused's power in that region?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Well, it did show me something. It showed me what I already knew, because as you yourself said, I was involved in all the negotiations, and I knew the people involved, and I knew that without the accused, nothing could be done. And so this was yet further confirmation of that. If you needed to have any proof, it was confirmation of what we all knew already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you set out that later on the accused's attitude toward Martic was somewhat different, and he described him in unappealing terms, I think.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely right. Those assessments and his approach to people generally -- well, the accused would change his approach to people. And as Martic was in favour of certain steps or didn't follow the lines of the policies pursued by the accused, so then the accused said, "He's an idiot. He ought to be arrested. He's doing silly things." So that was the time when he gave instructions for the bombing of Zagreb, which compromised, absolutely compromised overall Serb policies, because the international community viewed this in its entirety, as a comprehensive phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In writing, you deal with a meeting you and Prime Minister Mile Akmadzic had with Karadzic and Krajisnik on the 3rd of December, 1993. Several days later on the 9th you met with the accused, David Owen, and Thorvald Stoltenberg. On this occasion you negotiated about granting Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Serbs access to the sea. In summary, can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a desire or, rather, condition for a peaceful solution, to give them an outlet or access to the sea, both to Republika Srpska and to the Muslims. And then -- I don't want to go into the details, the geographic details at this point, but it was to the very south, in the southernmost region of the Croatian coast, from Molunat to the Ostro promontory. And both sides or, rather, Republika Srpska wanted to have access to the sea there, and the Muslims insisted on having an outlet at Neum. However, in negotiations with the Serb leadership, what was stated was that we should offer both parties a part, a section and I must say that was only on the level of theoretical negotiations, because, of course, without parliament you couldn't give a single square kilometre of the coastline to anyone. But anyway, President Tudjman insisted on this and said that we're going to be in favour of that. "I'm going to put that view to parliament. If it were to be a global solution to all the misunderstandings and outlying issues with Serbia, the RS, RSK, and so on and between -- in order to arrive at a global solution."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The point is was Milosevic -- or one of the points is was Milosevic negotiating with you on behalf of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely right. He was very active in that respect, and he did negotiate. And I even think that he had authorisation, if I can use that term, to negotiate on behalf of Republika Srpska, because, for example, he said to me, "Well, why are you splitting hairs? You have thousands of kilometres of coastline and now you're splitting hairs over some 20 kilometres." That's the kind of thing he said on behalf of Republika Srpska and for their advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You make the point in paragraph 36 of your statement that all other Serbian leaders addressed Milosevic formally, the power of the accused, formally apart from Miomir Minic who was a person friend of yours, and on question of personal relationships, you move forward to 1995, and the RSK Prime Minister Borislav Mikelic visiting the accused in Belgrade, and you were astonished by something you saw.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was this -- well, I don't know whether Mr. Minic's first name is Miomir. But never mind, that's not important at this point. What happened is that one day I happened to be in the offers of the accused, and the telephone rang, and I understood that they were discussing topics about what should or should not be done by television and said over television, and I saw him use the familiar form of the second person singular. With everybody else, and you can see this from the taped telephone conversations and other things, but from what I was able to see myself --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I move you on to Mikelic, please, because we've had quite a lot of evidence about the accused's address. Borislav -- Borislav Mikelic in 1995.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'll tell you the following. So we discussed these problems about opening the motorway and the problems that were outstanding, and I said, "This quite simply can't be solved in this way." To which the accused said to his secretary, "Call Boro Mikelic up for me." And I was rather surprised, because in ten or 15 minutes' time, he arrived from somewhere in Belgrade. And when he saw me in the office, he said, "What are you doing here?" And the accused said to him, "Sit down. Sit here and listen and don't ask questions." But this was said in such a tone of voice that I saw their relationship and felt the kind of relationship they had, which was the relationship of a master towards -- not to use the word "servant," but a master towards people who had to listen to him and who were in his service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another incident, 12th of February, 1994, at a FRY delegation to Croatia. Was Zeljko Simic, the Yugoslav deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs, negotiating with Croats, with yourself or the Croats?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: I attended the meetings. I think he was the Foreign Minister, not the deputy Foreign Minister, but I'm not quite sure. So we can have that checked out. But he did come, and he was a guest of the service, of Mate Granic, the Foreign Minister. But I also took part in the negotiations. After that, we left the building of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to the presidential Dvori palace where Simic took me aside into a corner and said, "Listen here. I think it's in your best interests for me to be the Foreign Minister, because if you talk to anyone else and negotiate with anyone else, then you'll see that Milosevic has surrounded himself with Chetniks and you won't be able to get anywhere with them." And then he asked me personally to talk to the accused, because he said that, "The accused respects you, and it would be a good idea for you to tell him to keep me in that position, to keep me on."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Move on to the 13th of January, 1995, a meeting in Belgrade. I think if we can just summarise paragraph 39. Did he say something to you very briefly about what Martic and Babic had been doing at the beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that on two or three occasions he actually told me, "Take care, because Babic and Martic have already committed atrocities and they have nothing further to lose." So the accused was not quite specific as to what he meant when he said "atrocities," but quite certainly there was something in it, something there, and that was that the accused did like to replace people and then would accuse them of atrocities. They did commit some atrocities, but he wasn't specific as to tell me what those were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And on the question of replacing people, did he at this meeting say what the future held for Vladislav Jovanovic, the Foreign Minister?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I noticed at that meeting that we weren't getting anywhere with Jovanovic because he had a negative attitude in all the negotiations. And then he stopped me, the accused stopped me, and said, "I'm going to tell you something now, but I don't want you to repeat this to anyone. I don't want you to repeat it to the public." And then he said, "I will replace Jovanovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say anything more about how or why he was going to do that?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, he did. Or, rather, I think the reason, I told him, that is to say, that we couldn't negotiate with him was just one of the reasons. I don't know about the other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he also address you in what you describe as a long monologue, at the end of which did he say significant about Bosnia, saying something about the solution to the problem and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. He spoke to me about Bosnia, and that was the leitmotif of the accused's relationship with Bosnia. Now, as far as Sarajevo was concerned, he said, "Sarajevo is not a Serbian town," and in that sense -- or, rather, this was in the context of speaking about the subject of Serbs, Muslims, what was being offered them, whether what was being offered was qualitatively okay or quantitatively okay. And he said, "We're going to let them have Sarajevo. And apart from that, the Serbs don't have more than a 50 per cent right to Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he link the yielding of Sarajevo to an exchange for any other territory?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely right. There was mention of the eastern enclaves, for example. However, he was not -- or, rather, the accused wasn't along the lines of Karadzic's thinking, Karadzic to begin with, because he said to me, "Well, these enclaves to the east, we can let them have then, because anyway, they'll come to belong to Republika Srpska in due course and then Serbs -- to the Serbs generally." So he didn't want to have this as a condition and so have to compensate for giving them that. So he said, "Let them have it."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally as to Abdic in Western Bosnia. Did he say anything about him or his relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as Abdic is concerned, he would say to us, "Well, it's best for the SAO Krajina or, rather the area as it was called at the time, the regions there, for you to take them into Croatia so that they should be in a confederal relationship with Croatia." And to that I said, "Well, listen here. You must know that that is unacceptable, because in that case, you cross the RSK to be within a confederation with Croatia." And on the other hand, he said that he had good relations with Abdic, that Abdic came to see him from time to time, that Abdic was himself in a very difficult situation. And I remember very vividly him saying, "I have just given him an order -- given an order for him to be supplied with 12.000 blankets. So help him too. You can help him too."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Later the same day were you joined by Borislav Mikelic and did the topic turn to Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't tell you what period of time this was exactly now, but I do remember that the accused kept playing between Karadzic and Mladic, balancing the two, and that Borislav Mikelic told me, "Mladic is 200 per cent Milosevic's man, because I drove him to see him two days ago." I think that was in January, sometime in January 1995. As far as Karadzic is concerned, he said, "Karadzic is a lost man, but he doesn't know it yet. And I'll try and topple him, but I'll do so via people in Banja Luka, who are reasonable people." And he also said, "I have a meeting with 20 some people from Banja Luka in two days' time, and then this would give us a majority in parliament, and we would able to topple Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 44 -- before perhaps I'll come back to paragraph 43, but paragraph 44, did the accused say anything about Karadzic's political viability at that time and give you any advice as to what you should do so far as having contact with him?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. As regards his assessment of his future, it was absolutely negative. He said that he was a lost politician, as I have already said, but that he wasn't aware of it, and that as far as he was concerned, at the time, he was on an anti-Karadzic position. I don't know what else I could say about that except that the accused realised that in such a situation in Republika Srpska, he had to play the military card, and the absolute authority in the military was Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, briefly, paragraph 43. I think you asked the accused about Croats who disappeared, and he offered to help with their location. In the event, did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: There were two things. On a number of occasions, I spoke about the position of Croats in Serbia and said, "Well, do something, please." And the accused was surprised and he said the lady Minister in the area is a Hungarian, and she has a feeling for these things, et cetera. And then he said that the leader of the Croats in Serbia was Bela Tonkovic, and he said, "Tell him to come to see me tomorrow and I'll see to it." And then I said, "President, there are quite a number of people missing, and their families need to know where they are. So please do something for that information to be obtained." And he promised he would. However, I never saw any results of that promise. He never kept his promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In paragraph 45 you give an example of the accused's intervention in respect of trucks of seeds en route to the RSK that were stopped by the Croats, the accused coming on the telephone and asking what of you?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: A couple of hours prior to that I was in Belgrade, and I was returning at the Pleso airport in Zagreb, and the people from UNPROFOR told me, "Call up this number to reach Mr. Milosevic," a number in Belgrade. I even remember the number. It was 184-162 in Belgrade. And I called -- dialed the number. I got the secretary and then the accused also at the other end. And the accused said to me, "Listen, Hrvoje, there's three trucks at the border. Please let them through. These are trucks carrying seeds, et cetera." I said, "Fine, I'll check this, and if that is so, we'll let them pass," which is what we did. But I have to say that I was especially surprised that the president of the republic should intervene for three trucks. However, this illustrates to what extent the accused was involved in the RSK and, naturally, therefore, also in the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving to May 1995. In writing you set out how President Tudjman played recordings of two conversations intercepted between the accused and Perisic. But then on the morning of the 3rd, two days later, did the accused's office call you and did he sound upset and speak to you informally? And then tell us what he said.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was shortly after the Operation Flash. We were at lunch, and I was told by the protocol that President Milosevic was on the line, and I picked the receiver and I hear him telling me furiously, "Why are you doing this? Why did we spend so many hours in discussion?" And then I responded, "Well, President, you see what the situation is like with these Serbs in Krajina over which you have considerable influence.
