We can't achieve anything." And Croatia was in a position when it had to deal with the problem militarily. But I said, "Get Martic and Celeketic replaced." Celeketic in those days was the number one in the RSK army. "Replace them and then you will see that the situation will improve immediately." His response was, "How can you say that to me? I can't replace them because I didn't appoint them." And then he slammed the receiver down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on to August and September 1995. I can go straight, I think, to paragraph 49 for our purposes. Or indeed 50. Did you have a meeting with the accused in Belgrade on the 20th of September, 1995, where you speak about the organisation of the Bosnian state?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the accused's position?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Well, at that meeting, there was a discussion on the implementation of the decisions of the Contact Group and the liberation of 70 or 72 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was required by the Contact Group. Of course -- I'm sorry, could you give me the date, please? Could you repeat the date once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you because I think it's another meeting that you've got in mind much this is a meeting that happened before Dayton and where there was discussion about some everything the problem without the international community, if that triggers your memory.

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, it does. I'm sorry, I got confused over the dates. Actually, at that meeting the accused said to me, "Look, we've had enough of this, Hrvoje. Let's each of us take our part of Bosnia without the international community. The US," that is the America, "is cradling this bastard without themselves knowing what they're doing, nor are they familiar with our problems." At the conference, he says conference, he didn't mention Dayton but it was a reference to that, "Be along our lines. We are against an unitary Bosnia. Let it be a Bosnia of two entities and three nations in which all decisions will be taken by consensus." I think that that is the correct interpretation of the content of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a reference to what he described as the roof of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if so, what did he mean by what he said?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: What he meant was the roof should be as thin as possible, which meant that the institutions which would be a kind of roof authority or umbrella authority should be as weak as possible, as thin as possible, which would mean that the entities should have far greater authority and should not depend on the decisions of the central authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally for meetings from this statement, Kosovo on the 10th of March of 1998. Did you meet the accused for the last time, and did he say to you whether he was or was not going to establish a provincial parliament and what his attitude was?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: First of all, this was my last meeting with the accused when he was president of Yugoslavia, and I went there as the president of the auditors of our company INA. And through the ambassador, Zeljko Knezevic, who knew I was coming to Belgrade, he expressed the wish to meet with me. And among other things, we discussed Kosovo. And this was an unavoidable topic in those days. And he said that he would resolve the problem of Kosovo. Or, rather, I said, "Tell me what your views of Kosovo are, because people from the international community are coming to Croatia and asking us for our opinion." His response was, "We will organise a bicameral chamber in which there will be no outvoting, no possibility of outvoting one by the other." And I said, "Well, President, that's fine, but that is far less than the -- than what Kosovo had according to the 1974 constitution." He said, "Yes, but that was a mistake which we will not repeat at any cost."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From your meetings with the accused, you offer a characterisation that includes the phrase "two irons in the fire." Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: This was in connection with Bosnia on the one hand and the RSK on the other. On a number of occasions, I said that differences in the approach to the problem between Tudjman and Milosevic were that the former first wanted to resolve the problem of Croatia, whereas the accused wanted first to resolve the problem of Bosnia and then other matters. However, as the accused had 30 per cent of Croatian territory under occupation and about 70 per cent of Bosnia under occupation, then he was the boss as one might say in all those territories, and that is why as a figure of speech or a metaphor, if you like, I said that he held two prongs in the fire, that is, Croatia on the one hand and Bosnia-Herzegovina in the other, which of course facilitated his approach in all negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally paragraph 54. From your meetings -- finally for this statement, from your meetings with the accused, what was his view of the influence and effective influence of outsiders in the world who were interfering with what was going on?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: I think that he belittled other people. He even said that the international community didn't understand anything about our history or our problems, and so on, and they're interfering without knowing what they're talking about. And there was an example,, the well known Z-4 plan drafted by Peter Galbraith and Ahrens, and he said, "Those are those idiots Galbraith and Ahrens prepared them without knowing themselves what they were doing." So this attitude was a highly critical one towards those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next topics are the three additional meetings which I can deal with very briefly which are referred to in the summary. If I can return to those. I say nothing about any underlying materials for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just tell us please if there was three other meetings that you can help us with. On the 13th of March, 1995, at a meeting in the presidential palace of the late Tudjman, did you - paragraph 4 of the summary - remind the accused that he said that the Serbs had now the right to more than 50 per cent of Bosnia and thus meant that Serbia was becoming larger? Sorry. Beg your pardon. It wasn't a conversation with him. You were reporting this conversation to Mr. Tudjman. I'm grateful to Ms. Pack for correcting me. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: I do remember to the extent that after meetings with the accused, I immediately went to the presidential palace while what I had discussed was still fresh in my memory and what I could note down on the plane returning, but I didn't quite understand the specifics of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. What as you noted down on the plane was the accused's reaction to your proposition that even at 50 per cent of Bosnia, Serbia was going to become larger. Did he say something about what Juppe said to him?

utterances.speaker: HRVOJE SARINIC
utterances.text: Juppe? Oh, I see, Juppe. I'm sorry. I have to say that I noted this down in those discussions with the accused. I couldn't write down anything. I would just jot down a word or two on a piece of paper, and then on the flight back I would draft my notes while they -- it was still fresh in my memory. Juppe, as far as I can remember, was extremely upset and revolted by the positions of the Serbs in the RS regarding the opening of the Sarajevo airport. That is what I recollect very well. And he was highly critical and very rough in relation to Karadzic who refused to open the Sarajevo airport. As for the rest, I'm not quite sure about it, so I'm unable to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what time we're sitting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time is coming up. How much longer do you anticipate for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not very long at all. Can I explain the position? There's a small part of his evidence, the part we're at now, which will have to be done in private session pursuant to an order of the Court, and then that's -- and then production of all the exhibits is done by the 89(F) statements, although there's a question that we're going to ask the Chamber in respect of the production not just for identification but the full production of a very limited number of intercepts. The reason for that can be seen in the schedule of the witness who speaks not only of identifying two witnesses but also of having seen such intercepts contemporaneously. So that's the open issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We should also consider how long the accused should have in relation to this. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tomorrow, once the Prosecution have finished, you can take up two hours and a quarter, Mr. Milosevic, to examine as this matter. We will consider the matter, if necessary, any further. Mr. Sarinic, thank you for coming. Could I add this in your case, not, of course, to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and of course no one should try to talk to you about it. If there were anything, let us know. But if you would be back, please, at 9.00 tomorrow morning to conclude your evidence tomorrow. Thank you very much. We will adjourn now until 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of January, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
